blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A scatter diagram plots paired values of two quantitative variables as points on a two-dimensional graph, one variable on each axis, to show how they relate.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The charts in §4.2–4.3 show one variable at a time. The scatter diagram shows two measurements per person and lets the eye judge whether they rise together, move in opposite directions, or show no pattern.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Figure 4.8 plots weight against age for the 100 children in the under-five clinic register (ages 12–36 months, weights 8.6–15.4 kg). The cloud rises from lower left to upper right: older children tend to weigh more. Correlation (Chapter 11) puts a number on this and regression (Chapter 12) models it.

blocks.alt: Scatter diagram of age against weight
blocks.caption: Figure 4.8. Scatter diagram of weight against age, under-five clinic register (n = 100).

points.html: Look at the scatter diagram before you compute a correlation coefficient. A single number can mislead badly when the relationship is curved or driven by a few outliers.
Both variables must be quantitative. For a numeric outcome across the categories of a categorical variable, use side-by-side box plots (§4.3.4).
Put the explanatory variable (here, age) on the x-axis and the outcome (weight) on the y-axis.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 4.3

questions.prompt: A box plot’s median line sits much closer to the top of the box than the bottom. What does that tell you about the shape of the middle half of the data?
questions.answer: The distance from the median to Q3 is short and the distance from Q1 to the median is long, so the lower half of the middle 50% is more spread out. That is a sign of left (negative) skew within the IQR. Check the whiskers and outliers too before describing the whole distribution.

questions.prompt: For CBHI members, Q1 = 3.5 km and Q3 = 9.2 km, and distances run from 0.2 to 14.7 km. Compute the Tukey fences and say whether any member household would be drawn as a separate point.
questions.answer: IQR = 9.2 − 3.5 = 5.7 km; 1.5 × IQR = 8.55 km. Lower fence = 3.5 − 8.55 = −5.05 km; upper fence = 9.2 + 8.55 = 17.75 km. The minimum (0.2 km) and maximum (14.7 km) both lie inside, so no household is drawn separately, and the whiskers reach the minimum and the maximum. (With the unrounded Q3 of 9.175 km the fences are −5.01 and 17.69 km; the conclusion is the same.)

questions.prompt: Why might you prefer a stem-and-leaf plot to a histogram for a small dataset?
questions.answer: It shows the shape of the distribution and still keeps every value, so you can read back any observation and count the median and quartiles straight off it. A histogram loses the individual values once they are grouped. With a small dataset the individual values still carry information, and the plot stays short enough to read.
